sectionTitle: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Nanoscience refers to structures that are 1–100 nm in size, of the order of a few hundred atoms. Nanoparticles, are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5 ), which have diameters between 100 and 2500 nm (1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m). Coarse particles (PM₁₀ ) have diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Coarse particles are often referred to as dust.
As the side of cube decreases by a factor of 10 the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.

Nanoparticles may have properties different from those for the same materials in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio. It may also mean that smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
Students should be able to compare ‘nano’ dimensions to typical dimensions of atoms and molecules.

Nanoparticles have many applications in medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts. New applications for nanoparticulate materials are an important area of research.
Students should consider advantages and disadvantages of the applications of these nanoparticulate materials, but do not need to know specific examples or properties other than those specified.
given appropriate information, evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose
explain that there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should consider advantages and disadvantages of the applications of these nanoparticulate materials, but do not need to know specific examples or properties other than those specified.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this section asks a student to recall a named nanomaterial, a named brand of product, or any property beyond the two the specification itself supplies - that a high surface area to volume ratio can make properties differ from the bulk material, and that smaller quantities may be needed to be effective. The only applications taught are the six listed in 4.2.4.2: medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts. Where a substance appears in an evaluation question it is described generically (a metal oxide in a sun cream, a metal catalyst in a factory) and every fact needed to answer is printed in the stem, exactly as 'given appropriate information, evaluate' requires; nothing here can be answered only by a student who has memorised that example. Advantages and disadvantages are always weighed against one another rather than listed one-sidedly, and risks are always framed as possible rather than established.

concepts.definition: The study of structures that are 1–100 nm in size, of the order of a few hundred atoms. Such structures are far bigger than a single atom but far too small to be seen with a light microscope.
A particle in the 1–100 nm size range. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5) and contain of the order of a few hundred atoms.
Particles with diameters between 100 and 2500 nm (1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m). They are larger than nanoparticles and smaller than coarse particles.
Particles with diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Coarse particles are often referred to as dust.
One thousand-millionth of a metre, 1 x 10⁻⁹ m. A nanometre is one thousand times smaller than a micrometre, so 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m is the same length as 2500 nm.
The total surface area of an object divided by its volume. For a cube of side l it is 6l² ÷ l³, which equals 6 ÷ l, so the ratio rises as the cube gets smaller.
As the side of cube decreases by a factor of 10 the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.
The same substance in ordinary, much larger pieces. Its surface area to volume ratio is low, so its properties can differ from those of the identical material as nanoparticles.
The mass of a material needed to do a job. Because nanoparticles expose so much surface, smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
A single atom is roughly 0.1 nm across and small molecules are a fraction of a nanometre wide, so a 1 nm structure is only about ten atoms across and a 100 nm particle is hundreds of atoms across.
Nanoparticles have many applications in medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts. New applications are an important area of research.
A catalyst supplied as nanoparticles rather than as larger lumps or pellets. The very large surface area per gram means a smaller mass produces the same catalytic effect.
Weighing the advantages of a use of nanoparticles against its disadvantages, using only the information given, and reaching a judgement that refers to both sides.
A harm that might follow from using nanoparticles, for example effects on the body or the environment that have not yet been fully tested because the materials are new.

misconceptions.question: Which is smaller, a nanoparticle or a fine particle (PM2.5)?
misconceptions.correct: A nanoparticle. Nanoparticles are 1–100 nm across, while fine particles are 100 to 2500 nm.
misconceptions.misconception: Fine particles must be the smallest of the three categories, because 'fine' means the finest grade there is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of 'fine' is the smallest grade of anything - fine sand, fine flour - so students rank the categories by the sound of the word instead of by the diameters printed beside them.
misconceptions.correction: Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1–100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles up to 1 x 10⁻⁵ m. 'Fine' is only fine compared with dust.

misconceptions.question: What does the 2.5 in PM2.5 refer to?
misconceptions.correct: An upper diameter of 2.5 micrometres, that is 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m, or 2500 nm.
misconceptions.misconception: PM2.5 means the particles are 2.5 nm across, and PM₁₀ means they are 10 nm across.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other size in this topic is quoted in nanometres, so students assume the PM numbers must be nanometres too. That makes both PM classes look smaller than nanoparticles, reversing the whole size order.
misconceptions.correction: The PM numbers are in micrometres. PM2.5 is 2500 nm and PM₁₀ is 10 000 nm, so both classes are far larger than any nanoparticle.

misconceptions.question: How does the size of a nanoparticle compare with the size of one atom?
misconceptions.correct: A nanoparticle is much bigger: it is of the order of a few hundred atoms, and one atom is about 0.1 nm across.
misconceptions.misconception: A nanoparticle is a single atom, or a particle only one or two atoms wide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nano' is used loosely to mean 'as small as things get', and students meet 10⁻⁹ m and 10⁻¹⁰ m in the same breath, so the two scales collapse into one.
misconceptions.correction: One atom is roughly 0.1 nm, so even the smallest 1 nm structure is about ten atoms across, and a nanoparticle holds a few hundred atoms.

misconceptions.question: A cube's side is divided by 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
misconceptions.correct: The ratio increases by a factor of 10.
misconceptions.misconception: The ratio decreases, because a smaller cube obviously has a smaller surface area.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track the surface area alone and forget that the volume is falling faster than the area. Everything about the cube is getting smaller, so the ratio 'must' get smaller as well.
misconceptions.correction: Surface area falls by 100 but volume falls by 1000, so area ÷ volume rises tenfold. For a cube of side l the ratio is 6 ÷ l, which grows as l shrinks.

misconceptions.question: By what factor does the surface area to volume ratio change when the side is divided by 10?
misconceptions.correct: It increases by a factor of 10.
misconceptions.misconception: It increases by a factor of 100, because surface area depends on the square of the side.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 6l² in the surface area formula is the most memorable part, so students apply the squaring rule to the ratio itself and never divide by the l³ underneath it.
misconceptions.correction: Work with the whole ratio: 6l² ÷ l³ = 6 ÷ l. Only one power of l survives, so dividing the side by 10 multiplies the ratio by 10, not by 100.

misconceptions.question: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 1 cm?
misconceptions.correct: 6, because the surface area is 6 cm² and the volume is 1 cm³.
misconceptions.misconception: The answer is 1 ÷ 6, because you divide the volume by the surface area.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'surface area to volume' are read as a fraction with volume on top, or the two numbers are simply divided in whichever order gives a tidier-looking answer.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity named first goes on top: surface area ÷ volume. For a 1 cm cube that is 6 ÷ 1 = 6.

misconceptions.question: Why can nanoparticles behave differently from the same material in bulk?
misconceptions.correct: Because of their high surface area to volume ratio, a far greater fraction of their atoms sits at the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Because grinding a material down to the nanoscale turns it into a different substance made of different atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A change of property is assumed to require a chemical change, so students invent a new substance rather than accept that one substance can behave differently at a different size.
misconceptions.correction: The material is chemically identical - same element or compound, same formula. Only the surface area to volume ratio has changed, and that alone is enough to change the properties.

misconceptions.question: How does the mass of nanoparticles needed compare with the mass of the bulk material?
misconceptions.correct: Smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
misconceptions.misconception: You need a larger mass of nanoparticles, because each particle is so tiny that enormous numbers of them are required.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count particles rather than weighing them. It is true that far more particles are needed, but each one has almost no mass, so the total mass still falls.
misconceptions.correction: Compare masses, not particle counts. A gram of nanoparticles offers vastly more surface than a gram of the bulk solid, so less material does the same job.

misconceptions.question: Roughly how many atoms wide is a 1 nm structure?
misconceptions.correct: About ten, since a typical atom is around 0.1 nm across.
misconceptions.misconception: About a thousand, because a nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m and an atom is only 10⁻¹² m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The atomic diameter is misremembered as a picometre-scale number, so the gap between the nanoscale and the atomic scale is inflated by a factor of a thousand.
misconceptions.correction: Take an atom as roughly 0.1 nm, that is 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m. Divide 1 nm by 0.1 nm and you get about ten atoms across.

misconceptions.question: Where are nanoparticles used?
misconceptions.correct: In medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanoparticles are only used in research laboratories and have no uses in ordinary consumer products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'nanotechnology' sounds futuristic and experimental, so students file it under research only and overlook the sun cream and the deodorant already in the bathroom.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists everyday uses: medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts. New applications are also an important area of research.

misconceptions.question: Why is a catalyst often used as nanoparticles?
misconceptions.correct: The very high surface area per gram means a smaller mass of catalyst produces the same effect.
misconceptions.misconception: Because nanoparticles are chemically more reactive, so they are used up faster and that speeds the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More effective' is heard as 'more reactive', and the definition of a catalyst as unchanged at the end of the reaction is forgotten under the pressure of an unfamiliar context.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst is not used up at all. Splitting it into nanoparticles simply exposes far more surface for the reaction, so a smaller mass is needed.

misconceptions.question: What must an evaluation of a use of nanoparticles include?
misconceptions.correct: Both the advantages and the disadvantages given, and a judgement that refers to both of them.
misconceptions.misconception: An evaluation means listing every advantage you can find and then recommending the use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'evaluate' as 'justify', so the answer becomes one-sided: only the supporting evidence in the stem is used and the drawbacks printed alongside it are read past.
misconceptions.correction: Use the information on both sides, weigh one against the other, and state a conclusion that acknowledges the cost as well as the benefit.

misconceptions.question: Are the risks of using nanoparticles fully known?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are possible risks, and the long-term effects of many nanoparticles have not been fully tested.
misconceptions.misconception: There can be no risk, because the products are already on sale and so must have been proved completely safe.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being on sale is taken as proof of complete safety, and because these materials are new, long-term evidence has simply not had time to accumulate.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks you to explain that there are possible risks. Being in use shows a product met current rules, not that every long-term effect is known.

misconceptions.question: Why does the small size of nanoparticles create a possible risk?
misconceptions.correct: They are small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs or to pass into cells, where their effects are not fully known.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanoparticles are far too small to have any effect on the body, so they simply pass straight through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Small is equated with harmless. Because a nanoparticle is invisible, students assume the body cannot notice it, which reverses the actual concern that it reaches places larger particles cannot.
misconceptions.correction: It is the small size that causes the concern: nanoparticles can reach parts of the body that coarse particles never reach, and their high surface area makes them chemically active there.

mcqs.stem: Which particles have diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m?

options.text: Fine particles, which are known as PM2.5
options.rationale: 1 x 10⁻⁷ m to 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m is 100 to 2500 nm, the range the specification gives for fine particles.

options.text: Coarse particles, often called dust
options.rationale: Reading PM₁₀ as 10 nm makes coarse particles look like the smallest class, so the middle range is given to them.

options.text: Nanoparticles, which are 1–100 nm wide
options.rationale: A student who believes fine particles are the smallest class has to hand this larger range to nanoparticles instead.

options.text: Single atoms and simple molecules
options.rationale: Treating everything in this topic as atom-sized makes any quoted range look like the size of individual atoms.

mcqs.stem: A particle in smoke is measured and found to have a diameter of 5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Which class of particle is it?

options.text: A nanoparticle, 1 to 100 nm across
options.rationale: Students who rank the classes by name rather than by diameter treat anything invisible in smoke as a nanoparticle.

options.text: A coarse particle, often called dust
options.rationale: 5 x 10⁻⁶ m lies between 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m and 1 x 10⁻⁵ m, the coarse particle range, and coarse particles are often referred to as dust.

options.text: A fine particle, one of the PM2.5 class
options.rationale: Misreading the PM figures as nanometres puts a 5000 nm particle in PM2.5, although fine particles stop at 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m.

options.text: A single atom, about 0.1 nm wide
options.rationale: Collapsing the nanoscale onto the atomic scale makes any small measured diameter look like a single atom.

mcqs.stem: The side of a cube of a solid is decreased by a factor of 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?

options.text: It decreases by a factor of ten
options.rationale: Following the falling surface area alone, and ignoring that the volume falls faster, points the change the wrong way.

options.text: It increases by one hundred times
options.rationale: Applying the squaring rule for area to the whole ratio gives 100 instead of 10.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 10
options.rationale: The ratio for a cube of side l is 6l² ÷ l³ = 6 ÷ l, so dividing the side by 10 multiplies the ratio by 10.

options.text: It stays the same, both fall
options.rationale: Treating area and volume as interchangeable makes the two changes look as though they cancel out.

mcqs.stem: A cube of side 1 cm has a surface area to volume ratio of 6. What is the ratio for a cube of side 0.1 cm?

options.text: 6, unchanged by the cutting up
options.rationale: Reading the ratio as a fixed property of the substance rather than of the size leaves it untouched.

options.text: 600, a hundred times bigger than 6
options.rationale: Squaring the scale factor because surface area depends on l² multiplies the ratio by 100 instead of 10.

options.text: 0.6, ten times less than before
options.rationale: Assuming a smaller cube must have a smaller ratio divides by 10 rather than multiplying.

options.text: 60, ten times the first cube
options.rationale: The ratio is 6 ÷ l, so a side of 0.1 cm gives 6 ÷ 0.1 = 60: as the side falls by 10 the ratio rises by 10.

mcqs.stem: Nanoparticles of a metal can behave differently from a lump of the same metal. Why?

options.text: They are a more reactive element than the metal
options.rationale: A related version of the same error: the nanoparticles are treated as a new, more reactive element.

options.text: They have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
options.rationale: The specification attributes the different properties to the high surface area to volume ratio of nanoparticles.

options.text: They are built from different atoms than the lump
options.rationale: Assuming a property change needs a chemical change turns the nanoparticles into a different substance.

options.text: They each contain fewer than roughly ten atoms
options.rationale: Nanoparticles are of the order of a few hundred atoms, not a handful, so this confuses nano with atomic scale.

mcqs.stem: A sun cream can be made using a metal oxide in bulk form or as nanoparticles of the same oxide. Compared with the bulk form, the mass of the nanoparticle form needed to protect the skin is:

options.text: larger, since each particle is so very tiny
options.rationale: Counting particles instead of weighing them makes the huge number of nanoparticles look like a larger mass.

options.text: the same, because the oxide is unchanged
options.rationale: Correctly noting that the chemical is identical, but wrongly concluding that nothing about its behaviour can differ.

options.text: smaller, as far more surface gets exposed
options.rationale: The specification states that smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.

options.text: larger, as less surface area is exposed
options.rationale: Assuming that a smaller particle must expose less surface - the same error as with the shrinking cube - leads to more material being thought necessary.

mcqs.stem: A typical atom has a diameter of about 0.1 nm. Roughly how many atoms would fit across a structure 1 nm wide?

options.text: About a thousand atoms wide
options.rationale: Taking an atom as 10⁻¹² m rather than 10⁻¹⁰ m inflates the gap between the two scales a thousandfold.

options.text: About one hundred atoms
options.rationale: A milder version of the same scale error, using 0.01 nm for the diameter of an atom.

options.text: One atom: 1 nm is one atom
options.rationale: Equating the nanoscale with the atomic scale makes a 1 nm structure a single atom.

options.text: About ten atoms in a row
options.rationale: 1 nm ÷ 0.1 nm = 10, so a 1 nm structure is only about ten atoms across.

mcqs.stem: A nanoparticle is 20 nm across. A typical atom is about 0.1 nm across. Roughly how many atoms lie along one edge of the nanoparticle?

options.text: About 20 atoms across
options.rationale: Treating one nanometre as the width of one atom collapses the nanoscale onto the atomic scale.

options.text: About 200 atoms across
options.rationale: 20 nm ÷ 0.1 nm = 200, so the particle is a few hundred atoms across, as the specification says.

options.text: About 2000 atoms across
options.rationale: A milder form of the same scale error, taking an atom as 0.01 nm instead of 0.1 nm.

options.text: About 20 000 atoms across
options.rationale: Taking an atom as 10⁻¹² m rather than 10⁻¹⁰ m inflates the gap between the scales a thousandfold.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives only applications of nanoparticles named in the specification?

options.text: Medicines, fertilisers, road salt, alloys, water pipes
options.rationale: Substituting familiar bulk-chemistry uses for the named nanoparticle applications.

options.text: Research laboratories and specialised university work
options.rationale: Nanotechnology is filed under research alone, so everyday consumer products are overlooked.

options.text: Medicine, electronics, sun creams, deodorants, catalysts
options.rationale: These are exactly the applications the specification lists for nanoparticles.

options.text: Electronics, cement, steel making, glass, plastics
options.rationale: One correct application is padded out with heavy industries that do not appear in the specification.

mcqs.stem: A sun cream made with nanoparticles of a metal oxide is clear on the skin and blocks more ultraviolet light than the bulk form, but its long-term effects on skin cells have not yet been fully tested. Which is the best evaluation?

options.text: It should be banned, since untested means it is known to be harmful
options.rationale: Turns an untested effect into a proven harm, which the information given does not support.

options.text: It should be used, because it blocks the most ultraviolet light
options.rationale: A one-sided answer that treats 'evaluate' as 'justify' and ignores the drawback printed in the stem.

options.text: There is nothing to pick, as both creams act in the same way
options.rationale: Denies that the same oxide can behave differently at the nanoscale, contradicting the stem.

options.text: Better protection and appearance, but long-term effects untested
options.rationale: Uses both sides of the information given and reaches a judgement that names the benefit and the uncertainty.

mcqs.stem: A factory can buy a catalyst as 5 kg of pellets or as 50 g of nanoparticles that speed the reaction just as much. The nanoparticle form costs more per gram. Which evaluation uses this information best?

options.text: Much less mass is needed, so a higher price per gram may pay off
options.rationale: Weighs the hundredfold smaller mass against the higher unit price, exactly as the information invites.

options.text: Neither wins, since a catalyst cannot change the reaction rate
options.rationale: Contradicts the stem, which states both forms speed the reaction equally.

options.text: Nanoparticles are better, since they are used up much more slowly
options.rationale: A catalyst is not used up at all, so this reason is not available for either form.

options.text: The pellets are better, because the nanoparticles cost more per gram
options.rationale: Uses one figure only; the far smaller mass required is ignored, so the comparison is one-sided.

mcqs.stem: Why do scientists say there are possible risks in using nanoparticles?

options.text: They are on sale already, which proves they are safe
options.rationale: Being on sale shows current rules were met, not that every long-term effect has been tested.

options.text: They may enter cells and effects are not known
options.rationale: Their size lets them reach places larger particles cannot, and the long-term effects have not been fully tested.

options.text: They are far too small to affect the body's cells
options.rationale: Equates small with harmless, reversing the real concern about nanoparticles entering cells.

options.text: They are used up in reactions, leaving a harmful waste
options.rationale: Borrows the idea that nanoparticles are used up in the reaction and turns it into a supposed source of harmful waste; a catalyst is not used up at all.
